pumac-2019-finals-b-01.title: Mod 3, then factor a difference of squares
pumac-2019-finals-b-01.body:
**$n$ is even.** Modulo $3$: $7^m+9\equiv1$, while $2^n\equiv(-1)^n$. So $n$ is even, $n=2k$.

**Factor.** $7^m=2^{2k}-9=(2^k-3)(2^k+3)$. Both factors are positive (as $7^m\ge1$) and their product is a power of $7$, so each is a power of $7$. Their difference is $6$; their gcd divides $6$ and is a power of $7$, so it is $1$. Hence the smaller factor is $7^0=1$: $2^k-3=1$, $k=2$. Then $2^k+3=7=7^m$ gives $m=1$, $n=4$.

Check: $2^4=16=7+9$. ✓ So the only solution is $(n,m)=(4,1)$. ∎

pumac-2019-finals-b-01.title: Mod 3 and mod 8 (official)
pumac-2019-finals-b-01.body: As before $n=2k$ and $(2^k-3)(2^k+3)=7^m$, so $2^k-3$ and $2^k+3$ are both powers of $7$. If $k\ge3$, then $2^k-3\equiv5\pmod8$, but powers of $7$ are $\equiv1$ or $7\pmod 8$ — impossible. So $k\in\{0,1,2\}$: $k=0$ gives $2^0-3<0$; $k=1$ gives $-1$; $k=2$ gives $1\cdot7=7^1$. Hence $(n,m)=(4,1)$ is the unique solution. ∎

pumac-2019-finals-b-02.title: Handshake lemma and symmetric difference of paths
pumac-2019-finals-b-02.body:
**Only if.** If every vertex has odd degree in $H$, then $\sum_{v}\deg_H(v)=2|F|$ is even, and a sum of $|V|$ odd numbers is even only when $|V|$ is even.

**If.** Let $|V|=2k$ and split $V$ into pairs $\{u_1,w_1\},\dots,\{u_k,w_k\}$. Since $G$ is connected, choose a path $P_i$ from $u_i$ to $w_i$. In the path $P_i$ the endpoints have degree $1$ and every other vertex on it has degree $2$; so, as a set of edges, $P_i$ gives odd degree exactly at $u_i$ and $w_i$.

Let $F=P_1\,\triangle\,P_2\,\triangle\cdots\triangle\,P_k$ (an edge is in $F$ iff it lies in an odd number of the paths). For each vertex $v$, $\deg_F(v)\equiv\sum_i\deg_{P_i}(v)\pmod 2$, because an edge at $v$ used by $t$ paths contributes $t$ to the right side and $t\bmod 2$ to the left. Each vertex is an endpoint of exactly one path, so the right side is odd. Thus every vertex has odd degree in $(V,F)$. ∎

pumac-2019-finals-b-02.title: Spanning tree construction
pumac-2019-finals-b-02.body:
(Necessity as before.) For sufficiency, take a spanning tree $T$ of $G$ and let $F$ be the set of tree edges $e$ such that deleting $e$ from $T$ leaves two components of odd size. (Since $|V|$ is even, the two sides are both odd or both even.)

Fix a vertex $v$ with tree neighbours $x_1,\dots,x_d$, and let $s_i$ be the size of the component of $T-v$ containing $x_i$. The edge $vx_i$ splits $T$ into parts of sizes $s_i$ and $|V|-s_i$, so $vx_i\in F$ iff $s_i$ is odd. Now $s_1+\dots+s_d=|V|-1$ is odd, so an odd number of the $s_i$ are odd, i.e. $\deg_F(v)$ is odd. This holds for every $v$. ∎

pumac-2019-finals-b-03.title: Coordinates centred at $S$
pumac-2019-finals-b-03.body:
It suffices to show $\frac1{d_A}-\frac1{d_C}=\frac1{d_B}-\frac1{d_D}$, i.e. that for a chord through $S$ with one end ($A$ or $B$) on a fixed side of $MN$, $\frac1{d_{\text{that end}}}-\frac1{d_{\text{other end}}}$ does not depend on the chord.

Put $S$ at the origin with $MN$ on the $x$-axis, $M=(-a,0)$, $N=(a,0)$, and the side containing $A,B$ as $y>0$. The centre is $(0,k)$ for some $k$, so $\Gamma:\ x^2+y^2-2ky-a^2=0$.

A line through $S$ with direction $(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$, $0<\theta<\pi$, meets $\Gamma$ at the points $t(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$ with
$$t^2-2kt\sin\theta-a^2=0,\qquad t_1+t_2=2k\sin\theta,\quad t_1t_2=-a^2 .$$
So one root $t_1>0$ (the end above $MN$, e.g. $A$) and one $t_2<0$ (e.g. $C$), with $d_A=t_1\sin\theta$ and $d_C=-t_2\sin\theta$. Hence
$$\frac1{d_A}-\frac1{d_C}=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\left(\frac1{t_1}+\frac1{t_2}\right)=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\cdot\frac{t_1+t_2}{t_1t_2}=\frac{2k\sin\theta}{-a^2\sin\theta}=-\frac{2k}{a^2},$$
independent of $\theta$. Applying this to the chords $AC$ and $BD$ gives $\frac1{d_A}-\frac1{d_C}=\frac1{d_B}-\frac1{d_D}$, which rearranges to the claim. ∎

pumac-2019-finals-b-03.title: Similar triangles and power of a point (official)
pumac-2019-finals-b-03.body:
Again we show $\frac1{d_A}-\frac1{d_C}$ is constant. Let $O$ be the centre, $\theta$ the angle between $AC$ and $MN$, and suppose $AS\le CS$. From the similar right triangles formed by $A$, $C$, their feet on $MN$ and $S$, $\frac{d_A}{AS}=\frac{d_C}{CS}=\sin\theta$. Hence
$$\frac1{d_A}-\frac1{d_C}=\frac{1}{d_A}\cdot\frac{CS-AS}{CS}.$$
Let $P$ be the point on segment $CS$ with $CP=AS$; then $CS-AS=SP$, and $SP$ is twice the distance from $S$ to the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ to $AC$. Since $OS\perp MN$, the angle between $OS$ and $AC$ is $90^\circ-\theta$, so $SP=2\,OS\sin\theta$. With $d_A=AS\sin\theta$ and the power of the point $S$, $AS\cdot CS=MS\cdot NS$:
$$\frac1{d_A}-\frac1{d_C}=\frac{2\,OS\sin\theta}{AS\sin\theta\cdot CS}=\frac{2\,OS}{MS\cdot NS},$$
which depends only on $MN$ (when $AS>CS$ the same computation gives the negative of this; the sign is determined by which side of $MN$ the centre lies on, the same for both chords). Hence $\frac1{d_A}-\frac1{d_C}=\frac1{d_B}-\frac1{d_D}$. ∎
